terms.definition: End Of Day — a deadline meaning by the close of today (often local business hours).
Close Of Business — the end of the working day, commonly 5pm local time.
End Of Week — a deadline meaning by Friday / the end of the working week.
Objectives and Key Results — a goal-setting framework pairing an ambition with measurable results.
Key Performance Indicator — a metric chosen to track progress toward a goal.
Return On Investment — the gain from an investment relative to its cost.
Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization — a proxy for a company's core operating profit.
Compound Annual Growth Rate — the smoothed yearly growth rate of a value over a period.
Capital Expenditure — money spent on long-term assets like buildings or equipment.
Operating Expenditure — ongoing day-to-day running costs like salaries and rent.
Profit and Loss — a statement summarizing revenues, costs and profit over a period.
Business-to-Business — selling products or services to other companies rather than consumers.
Business-to-Consumer — selling directly to individual end users.
Software as a Service — software delivered over the internet on a subscription.
Annual Recurring Revenue — the yearly value of subscription contracts.
Monthly Recurring Revenue — the predictable subscription revenue earned each month.
Customer Acquisition Cost — the average spend to win one new customer.
Lifetime Value — the total revenue expected from a customer over the whole relationship.
The rate at which customers stop using or paying for a product.
How many months a company can keep operating before it runs out of cash.
How fast a company is spending its cash reserves, usually measured per month.
Go To Market — the plan for how a product reaches and sells to customers.
Total Addressable Market — the total revenue opportunity if you captured 100% of demand.
Serviceable Addressable Market — the slice of the TAM you can actually reach with your model.
Serviceable Obtainable Market — the realistic share of the SAM you can win near-term.
Non-Disclosure Agreement — a contract to keep shared information confidential.
Memorandum Of Understanding — a non-binding agreement outlining intent between parties.
Statement Of Work — a document defining deliverables, timeline and scope of a project.
Request For Proposal — an invitation for vendors to bid on a defined piece of work.
For Your Information — shared so you're aware, with no action required.
Fiscal Year — a company's 12-month accounting period, which may not match the calendar year.
The number of employees, or the budgeted number of roles a team is allowed to hire.
The idea that combined efforts produce more value than the parts would separately (often used ironically).
To return to a topic or person later rather than dealing with it now.
The easiest wins that take little effort for a quick result.
To make a noticeable, measurable difference to a key metric.
To attempt something impossibly large in scope; a warning against over-reaching.
To move a side discussion out of the current meeting and handle it separately.
To have a brief check-in conversation to sync up.
A thorough, detailed examination of a topic.
In business slang, a person's available time and capacity to take on more work.
Anyone with an interest in or influence over a project's outcome.
Something preventing work from progressing until it's resolved.
A specific task assigned to someone with an expected outcome, often from a meeting.
A tangible output a project is expected to produce and hand over.
The gradual, uncontrolled expansion of a project's requirements beyond the original plan.
The single guiding metric or goal that aligns a team's efforts.
The minimum features or capabilities required just to compete in a market.
Value Proposition — the core reason a customer should choose your product.
Ideal Customer Profile — a description of the type of customer your product fits best.
Net Promoter Score — a metric of how likely customers are to recommend you.
Selling an existing customer a higher tier or larger version of what they already buy.
Selling an existing customer an additional, complementary product.
End Of Message — marks that the whole note fits in the subject line; also End Of Month in finance.
A fundamental change in approach or in the underlying assumptions of a field.
People physically present doing the actual hands-on work.
Something that adds worth beyond the basics; the extra benefit you bring.
Essential — something whose failure would break the whole operation.
Cash reserves kept on hand to invest when the right opportunity appears.
A favorable external condition that helps growth or progress.
An adverse external condition that slows growth or progress.
To unite and rally defensively in response to a threat or criticism.
To examine a problem one layer at a time to reach the core.
An obvious, major problem that everyone is avoiding talking about.
A method widely accepted as the most effective proven way to do something.
A rough, approximate estimate.
The value, skills or resources someone contributes to an effort.
To examine a topic in progressively greater detail.
To get everything organized and properly prepared before acting.
Something that significantly and decisively shifts the situation.
A fixed time at which you must end a meeting no matter what.
Bogged down in low-level details, or swamped and struggling to keep up.
To use a resource or advantage to maximum effect (a favorite business verb).
A deliberate, fundamental change in strategy or direction.
To increase or accelerate activity, output or staffing.
To float an idea to others to gauge their reaction.
The proprietary ingredient or advantage that makes something uniquely work.
One authoritative place where a given piece of data officially lives.
A clearly bounded area of responsibility or ownership.
To approach a problem in an unconventional, creative way.
One's area of expertise, strength or comfort.
An outcome that benefits all parties involved.
A high-level overview that ignores the fine details.
A quick, rough calculation done without precise data.
The very newest and riskiest technology or approach, ahead of the leading edge.
A company's defining strength — the thing it does better than rivals.
Business slang for going deeper into a specific point or topic.
A profound, far-reaching transformation.
Someone regarded as an authority whose ideas shape opinion in a field.
An easy, fast success that builds momentum or goodwill.
The regular rhythm at which meetings, releases or check-ins happen.
To get everyone to a shared baseline understanding before moving on.
To pause a topic deliberately and come back to it later.
Specific and concrete enough that someone can actually act on it.
Innovation that radically upends an existing market or way of doing things.
Getting people to agree on and pull toward the same direction or priorities.
Genuine agreement and commitment from the people whose support you need.
The careful investigation done before committing to a deal or decision.
The point where a product clearly satisfies strong demand in a real market.
A durable competitive advantage that protects a business from rivals.
A self-reinforcing loop where each success makes the next one easier.
The revenue and cost of a single unit (one customer or sale), showing if the model scales profitably.
A task requiring a large amount of effort or resources.
To set a higher standard of quality or performance.
Money your company owes to its suppliers and creditors.
Money owed to your company by its customers.
The purchase of one company, or its assets, by another.
Profiting from a price difference for the same asset across two markets.
Things a business owns that have value or future benefit.
An official inspection of a company's or individual's accounts.
A snapshot of a company's assets, liabilities and capital at a point in time.
Measuring your performance against competitors or industry standards.
A large, well-established and financially sound company.
A loan to a company or government that pays interest over a set term.
Building a startup with little outside money, relying on savings and revenue.
The point where revenues exactly cover costs — no profit, no loss.
A short-term loan that covers a gap until longer-term funds arrive.
An individual who invests their own money in a startup for a stake.
Money invested into a company or project by its owners.
The movement of money into and out of a business.
An asset pledged as security against a loan.
A basic, interchangeable good that's freely traded, like gold or oil.
The exclusive legal right to use and reproduce a created work.
A person or business you owe money to.
A person or business that owes money to you.
The decline in an asset's value over time, usually from wear and tear.
Spreading into new products, customers or markets to reduce risk.
A share of profits paid regularly by a company to its shareholders.
Cost savings gained as production or purchasing volume increases.
A company's total value including debt and excluding cash.
Ownership value — a company's assets minus its liabilities.
A plan for an owner or investor to leave a business and recoup value.
A cost that stays the same regardless of output, such as rent.
Contracts to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date.
Gross Domestic Product — the total value of goods and services an economy produces.
Sales minus the direct cost of goods, before overheads and tax.
An actively managed fund using varied, often risky strategies for high returns.
Acquiring a company against the wishes of its board.
A general rise in prices over time that reduces purchasing power.
Illegally trading shares using confidential, non-public information.
Being unable to pay debts as they fall due.
Creations of the mind — inventions, designs, brands — protected by law.
Acquiring a company largely with borrowed money.
What a business owes — its debts and obligations.
How easily an asset can be converted into cash.
The study of the economy as a whole.
Profit expressed as a percentage of revenue.
Dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs.
The portion of a market's total sales that one company controls.
The combining of two or more companies into one.
The study of the decisions of individual consumers and firms.
A market dominated by just a few firms.
Ongoing costs not tied directly to production, such as rent and admin.
A legal right granting sole use of an invention for a set period.
A central bank creating money to buy assets and stimulate the economy.
A sustained decline in economic activity, often two quarters of falling GDP.
The total income a business earns from sales over a period.
An owner of shares in a company.
Small and Medium-sized Enterprise — a smaller business by headcount or revenue.
The network of suppliers and steps that produce and deliver a product.
Operating without depleting resources or harming the environment.
One company buying control of another.
A legally registered brand name, logo or phrase.
A company's total sales over a period (also the rate at which staff leave).
Money invested in high-risk, high-growth startups in return for equity.
Cash available for day-to-day operations — current assets minus current liabilities.
The income from an investment as a percentage of its price.
Annual Percentage Rate — the yearly cost of borrowing including fees.
A company structure that limits the owners' personal liability.
